evals.prompt: I run the Helsinki Elixir evening, we've done 6 editions now. Last month 118 people RSVP'd, the room at our host's office seats 60, and 41 turned up. I ordered pizza for 118 and binned most of it, which cost us about 640 euros. For next month I'm capping RSVPs at 60 so it matches the room exactly, and I've budgeted food for 60. A friend who runs a bigger group told me free evening events run 40-50% no-show so I should just assume half won't come. What should my numbers actually be?
evals.expected_output: A corrected no-show plan: CNCF's ~30% planning figure named as the sourced default, the 40-50% figure rejected as folklore, the group's own measured show-up rate (41 of 118) preferred because six editions exist, overbooking kept instead of a capacity-matched cap, surplus routed to an auto-promoting waitlist, food sized on expected door count, and a reminder schedule ending with a release-your-spot request two hours out.
expectations: States the no-show planning figure as roughly 30% of RSVPs and attributes it to CNCF Community Groups
Rejects the 40-50% no-show figure explicitly as folklore with no named organization behind it
Derives the group's own show-up rate from the numbers given (41 of 118, roughly 35%) rather than assuming the imported figure applies
Prefers the group's own measured rate over CNCF's figure because six editions of door counts already exist
Uses the median of the group's trailing editions, not the mean, when setting the local rate
Rejects capping RSVPs at the 60-seat capacity, because overbooking to the no-show ratio is the point of the calculation
Routes the overbook surplus beyond room capacity to a waitlist that auto-promotes, rather than onto the RSVP list
Sizes the food order on expected door count rather than on RSVPs, and names catering the registration list as the most common budget mistake at this scale
Puts the food budget near 60 people, not 118
Includes a reminder roughly two hours before the event asking people who cannot come to release their spot
Frames the release request as freeing a seat for someone on the waitlist, not as guilt or a rebuke
Records the door count rather than the registration count in the edition log
Specifies vegan and vegetarian options and allergen labelling for the food

evals.prompt: Two of us want to start a Postgres group in Bratislava. Neither of us knows the audience yet, it's a brand new group, and the first event has to happen on 14 April because that's when the venue is free and we already announced the date publicly. We both have day jobs, realistically 3 hours a month each. I want to run a hands-on workshop every month because that's what I'd want to attend, and if that's too much we could just do an open space so nobody has to prepare anything. Which one?
evals.expected_output: An explicit format ranking with the workshop and the open space both deleted rather than demoted, the deletions named, the fixed date used to promote formats needing no confirmed speaker, effort and value emitted as separate orderings, and study group or anchor + lightning recommended.
expectations: Presents an explicit efficiency ordering of the formats rather than a flat menu, leading with anchor + lightning
Gives the ordering as anchor + lightning > study group > two-talk classic > open space > hands-on workshop
Deletes the hands-on workshop outright rather than demoting it, citing the roughly 3 hours a month per organizer ceiling
Deletes the open space outright rather than offering it as the zero-preparation option, because the room has never met each other
Says explicitly which formats it deleted, not only which it recommends
Explains that the fixed 14 April date promotes formats needing no confirmed speaker, because speaker sourcing is the one lead time that cannot be compressed
Recommends a study group or anchor + lightning as the realistic pick for this first edition
Emits effort and value as separate orderings rather than blending them into a single rank
Justifies the effort tie between study group and open space: neither needs a confirmed speaker nor any organizer-prepared material
Emits no compliance-cost axis for the format choice, since none of the formats changes what the group owes anyone
Warns that a workshop run monthly by a two-person team breaks the cadence within a quarter
States that ten to fifteen attendees is a real first edition rather than setting a larger turnout target

evals.prompt: I lead DevRel at Corvex, we sell an observability SDK. Leadership approved budget for "Corvex User Groups" in Milan, Krakow, Manchester and Austin, first dates locked six weeks out. We have zero volunteers in any of those cities. My plan: my two DevRel engineers fly out and run every evening themselves, two talks from our own engineers plus a roadmap update, and we recruit local people to book the rooms and call them the organizers. Long term I want these to graduate into independent community groups. Is that the right progression?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the maturity-ladder framing, the one genuine choice (vendor-backed chapter vs company-staffed series) ranked on efficiency, effort and compliance cost, the staffed series promoted anyway for this fixed date with no local organizers, the irreversibility asymmetry stated, and the mislabelled volunteer arrangement called out.
expectations: Rejects the framing that the three host models form a maturity ladder or a progression toward independence
Notes that vendor-affiliated user groups predate the independent volunteer model, citing SHARE founded in 1955, so independence is not a later stage
States that no efficiency ranking applies across all three models, because the model is settled by who is asking rather than chosen
Identifies the one real choice available here as vendor-backed volunteer chapter versus company-staffed series
Gives efficiency as vendor-backed volunteer chapter > company-staffed series
Gives effort as company-staffed series > vendor-backed volunteer chapter
Gives compliance cost as company-staffed series > vendor-backed volunteer chapter
Explains the compliance line as the review each model triggers: a staffed series puts attendee data, the code of conduct and stage content under company legal and brand sign-off
Promotes the company-staffed series for this case anyway, because the date is fixed and no local organizer exists yet
States the irreversibility asymmetry: a staffed series can hand over to volunteers later, but a chapter cannot be un-handed
Calls out that recruiting locals to book rooms with no program control gives them an organizer's workload and a helper's authority
Requires at least one speaker per edition with no stake in Corvex's product, or accepts that attendance decays to customers only
Warns against the "user group" label while running a company-staffed series, and says to either give volunteers program control or drop the framing

evals.prompt: Putting together a one-pager to send to three companies I want as venue hosts for our Ghent Kotlin meetup. I want it to look credible so I wrote: "Industry benchmarks for developer meetups: 70% show-up rate, 40% repeat attendance, at least 1 in 3 speakers sourced from the audience, and groups should keep 2 editions of confirmed speakers ahead." We've run 9 editions so I do have our real numbers, they're just less flattering. Can you tighten the wording?
evals.expected_output: Every one of the four quoted figures relabelled as a baseline rather than an industry benchmark, the 70% shown to be arithmetic on CNCF's 30% no-show figure, the genuinely sourced figures listed as the ones safe to quote externally, and the group's own nine editions of measured numbers made the lead.
expectations: Refuses to present the 70% show-up rate, the 40% repeat attendance, the 1-in-3 room-sourced speakers and the 2-editions-ahead figures as industry benchmarks
Labels each of those four figures as a baseline rather than a measured industry figure
Explains the 70% show-up rate is the direct arithmetic complement of CNCF's roughly 30% no-show figure, not an independent finding
Tells the user to write "our target" instead of "industry benchmark" for any baseline
Warns that a baseline presented as an industry standard costs the user's credibility across the whole document

Names sourced figures safe to quote externally, including CNCF's 90-day inactivity threshold, its minimum of six meetings per calendar year, its bar of more than 10 attendees, and its 15-minute sponsor stage cap
Names DevOpsDays' published positions (no bought speaker slots, no distribution of attendee contact information) as quotable sourced material
Notes the 1-in-3 room-sourced speaker target is deliberately ambitious against Nielsen's participation rates rather than a typical outcome
Attributes the 90-9-1 participation inequality to Jakob Nielsen and 2006
Recommends leading the venue-host one-pager with the group's own nine editions of measured numbers, unflattering or not
Says which kind each number is whenever one is quoted, rather than presenting a mixed list unlabelled
Tells the user to replace the baselines with the group's own trailing three-edition median now that nine editions exist

evals.prompt: Our Vienna Scala meetup is in trouble. Last three door counts were 45, then 26, then 12. The last event was 118 days ago. I'm the only organizer left since Marek changed jobs. Repeat attendance was 18% the last time I checked. Our last sponsor did a 30-minute product demo because they paid for the drinks. My reset plan: book the 200-seat auditorium at the university, land a well-known keynote speaker, charge 10 euros a ticket so people actually show up, and rebrand as "Scala Vienna Conf". Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: The scale-up plan refused, the failing scorecard lines named against their thresholds, and an ordered repair starting with a co-organizer recruited from the regulars, then a fixed date and booked room before any speaker, a no-speaker fallback format, a published sponsor stage cap, and a holdable cadence.
expectations: Refuses the bigger venue, the keynote and the rebrand as the reset, and says to fix the failing lines before adding any scale
Flags the 118-day gap as past CNCF's 90-day inactivity threshold
Flags that a single organizer is one job change from dead, and makes recruiting a second organizer the first action
Sources that second organizer from the remaining regulars rather than from an open public call
Gives the repair in order: recruit a co-organizer, fix a date and book the room, pick a no-speaker-needed fallback format, cap sponsor stage time, restart at a holdable cadence
Tells the user to fix the date and book the room before finding a speaker, not after
Names a fallback format that needs no external speaker, such as a study group, demo night or open space
Connects the 30-minute sponsor demo to the 18% repeat attendance as cause rather than coincidence
Caps sponsor stage time at 15 minutes or less, publishes the cap, and holds it
Marks 18% repeat attendance as failing against a 40% target and identifies that 40% as a baseline, not an industry figure
Declines to treat paid tickets as the no-show fix, pointing instead to overbooking, an auto-promoting waitlist and reminders
States that the restarted cadence must be one the remaining organizers can hold when tired, because a missed edition costs more trust than a slower cadence

evals.prompt: Every month it's the same. Three weeks before our Manchester Go evening I start messaging people asking if anyone can talk. I've cancelled twice this year when nobody said yes. I post an open call on LinkedIn and in our Slack every month and get basically nothing back. Should I be posting earlier, or switching to a panel discussion whenever I can't find a speaker? We're at edition 19.
evals.expected_output: A standing speaker pipeline replacing the monthly plea: permanent CFP, direct named asks with a short slot, conference harvesting, neighbouring-group trades, lightning slots that manufacture future anchors, a board tracking two editions ahead, a no-speaker fallback format kept in the plan, and the panel-as-fallback rejected.
expectations: Replaces the monthly open call with a standing call for proposals: a permanent form linked from every event page and every announcement
Explains that an open call only reaches people who already consider themselves speakers, so direct asks to named regulars convert far better
Scripts the direct ask around a short, named slot length, for example five minutes on what they built
Recommends harvesting speakers from regional conferences, because an already-given talk repeats locally with no new preparation
Says to ask conference speakers during or in the week of that conference, while it is fresh
Recommends trading speakers with neighbouring groups one city or one technology over, cross-promoting both audiences
Sets the pipeline target at two confirmed editions ahead
States the board's three states: two editions ahead is healthy, one ahead is a warning, zero ahead is a fire
Keeps a no-speaker-needed fallback format in the plan so a cancellation costs a format change rather than an edition
Rejects booking a panel because no speaker was found, naming it as a failure pattern rather than a fallback
Recommends a visible pipeline board tracking confirmed, provisional and prospect speakers per date
Recommends anchor + lightning so an edition needs one confirmed speaker instead of two, and so each lightning slot produces a candidate anchor speaker for a later edition

evals.prompt: Nice problem to have: Trelix, a monitoring vendor, offered 3,600 euros to sponsor our Copenhagen Python meetup for a full year. Their terms are a 30-minute technical session at every edition given by their solutions architect, the RSVP list exported to them after each event so their SDR can follow up, and badge scanning at the door. That covers food for the whole year and I'd stop paying out of pocket. I was going to counter at 20 minutes and give them only the email addresses of people who tick a box on the RSVP form. Fair deal?
evals.expected_output: The bought slot refused outright rather than negotiated down, the attendee-list export refused including the tick-box subset, badge scanning made opt-in, the published stage cap applied, the sponsor's speaker routed through the normal content filter, and the cost-base risk of a year funded by one sponsor flagged.
expectations: Refuses the guaranteed session in exchange for money outright, rather than negotiating its length down to 20 minutes
Quotes DevOpsDays' position that no speaker spots can be bought by sponsors, ever
Caps any sponsor stage time at 15 minutes as CNCF's published ceiling
Notes DevOpsDays holds its own sponsors to a shorter bar, a short elevator pitch on the order of a minute or two
Tells the user to pick a cap, publish it, and hold it rather than negotiating it per sponsor
Refuses to export the RSVP list, including the tick-box-filtered subset handed over by the organizers
States the sponsor earns contacts at their own table through an explicit opt-in, never through an organizer-supplied list
Rejects badge scanning as a default and makes it opt-in only
Routes Trelix's solutions architect through the same content review as any other speaker, with no guaranteed slot
Applies the code of conduct to sponsor staff, including recruiters
Warns that a year of food funded by one sponsor raises the cost base, so losing them would cost the group rather than one edition's food
Recommends stating the conduct rules in writing before accepting anything from Trelix
Recommends rotating venue and food hosts rather than binding a full year to a single sponsor

evals.prompt: Situation at our Zurich Kafka meetup. Nomatic hosts us, their office, their pizza, every month for the last eight editions. Two of our three organizers work at Nomatic. Their head of product now wants a standing 25-minute slot each edition called "What's new in Nomatic" and says that's fair given they cover everything. Attendance is holding at 34-38 so I don't think it's actually hurting us. They send slides the morning of the event, sometimes not at all. How do I handle this?
evals.expected_output: The pitch filter applied with its repairs in order, the 25-minute standing slot cut to the published cap, slides required in advance, the organizer-employer concentration flagged against CNCF's 50% cap, one non-host speaker per edition required, venue rotation and season-length booking recommended, and flat attendance rejected as proof of health.
expectations: Applies the pitch test: could this talk be given by someone who does not sell this product?
Gives the repairs in order of preference: reframe around the problem keeping the product as setting, move the product content into a short sponsor slot, decline
Cuts the slot to five minutes or to the published sponsor cap rather than leaving it at 25 minutes
Requires the title, the one-line takeaway and the slides in advance from every speaker including this one
Names the morning-of deck as how a group discovers on stage that the talk was a product demo
Flags that two of three organizers from Nomatic breaches CNCF's cap of 50% of an organizer team from any one company
Requires at least one speaker per edition with no stake in the host's product
Recommends rotating venue hosts rather than staying with Nomatic indefinitely
Books venue hosts a season at a time, roughly three editions, rather than a full year
Warns that a single host that also employs half the organizers turns the group into that company's user group whatever anyone intended
Rejects flat attendance of 34-38 as evidence the arrangement is harmless, and points at repeat attendance and new faces as the signals that move first
Notes that regulars who stop coming over this will not say why
Recommends publishing the stage-time cap so it applies to Nomatic identically to any other sponsor

evals.prompt: Our Sao Paulo Kubernetes group pulls 40-55 people every month and has for a year. But the same four people do everything: me, two friends who help at the door, and one guy who always volunteers to speak. Everyone else shows up, eats, and leaves. My board wants a plan to convert the lurkers, so I was thinking a points system, badges for attending three in a row, and a leaderboard on our site. What would you do?
evals.expected_output: The 90% lurker share normalised against Nielsen's participation inequality, the gamification plan rejected, and the attendee-to-co-organizer ladder given with each rung recruited from the one below, mapped onto the Orbit Model with its status noted, plus direct asks, real volunteer ownership and public co-organizer recruitment and exit.
expectations: States that roughly 90% lurking is normal rather than a failure of the program, citing Nielsen's 90-9-1 participation inequality
Dates the 90-9-1 finding to 2006
Reframes the goal away from converting lurkers and toward lowering the barrier to the next rung
Rejects the points system, the badges and the leaderboard as the intervention
Gives the ladder as attendee, regular, lightning speaker, volunteer, co-organizer
States each rung is recruited from the one directly below it
Maps the ladder onto the Orbit Model's four levels: Explorers, Participants, Contributors, Advocates
Gives Orbit's gravity definition as love multiplied by reach
Notes Orbit was published in 2019 and is no longer actively developed, citing it as a stable framework rather than a live product
Recommends asking named regulars directly, for example whether they would do five minutes on what they built, instead of an open call
Gives volunteers one or two real ownership areas each, such as food, A/V, emcee or socials, rather than ad-hoc help
Recruits co-organizers publicly and on a low bar, approved when at least half the current organizers say yes
Handles organizer departures publicly too, so a silent exit does not leave a ghost owner on the group's accounts

evals.prompt: It's just me and my colleague Priya running a new AI infrastructure meetup in Bangalore. We did edition one last week, 34 people through the door, it went great. We're both hyped and want to go weekly to build momentum while the energy is there. We have nobody lined up past edition two. If weekly turns out to be too much we figured we'd just run it whenever we happen to find a good speaker. Also should we alternate weekdays so more people can make at least one?
evals.expected_output: Weekly rejected for a two-person team with no pipeline, speaker-driven scheduling rejected as cadence collapse, a single fixed recurring slot recommended over alternating days, and CNCF's published cadence thresholds given: monthly ideal, 90-day inactivity, six meetings a year, quarterly with more than 10 attendees.
expectations: Rejects weekly as the cadence for a two-person team with no speaker pipeline
Rejects "whenever we find a speaker" as a cadence and names it as how a cadence collapses
Tells them to fix the slot, book the room, then fill the program, rather than letting the speaker set the date
Rejects alternating weekdays and recommends a single recurring predictable slot such as second Tuesday at 19:00
Explains that a fixed slot becomes a habit and removes one decision per edition
Gives CNCF's Tuesday-to-Thursday evening after-work default, adjusted to local culture
Names CNCF's ideal cadence as monthly
Names CNCF's inactivity threshold: more than 90 days between events marks a chapter inactive
Names CNCF's minimum of at least six meetings per calendar year for technical groups
Names CNCF's active-status bar as a quarterly event with more than 10 attendees, and states that the figure counts attendees rather than registrations
States that below quarterly a group has occasional events rather than a program
Warns that a missed edition costs more trust than a slower cadence, so they should not commit to monthly until the pipeline supports it

evals.prompt: I need something to put in front of my manager on Monday. It's a new meetup for our platform team's open-source project, first edition in Lisbon in October. Give me the full twelve-month programme, all twelve dates with the topic and speaker for each, plus which sponsor covers which month. Please don't ask me questions, just produce it and I'll correct whatever's wrong.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to invent twelve editions, the gating interview run one question at a time before any format is proposed, and the deliverables produced in order starting with a charter naming exactly one SPACES outcome, an edition plan only three deep with everything beyond marked provisional, plus pipeline board, edition log skeleton and a scorecard baseline reading "not measured yet".
expectations: Refuses to invent twelve editions of topics, speakers and sponsors
Plans three editions deep and marks everything beyond edition three as provisional
Asks the gating interview questions before proposing a format, rather than producing a format on no information
Asks one question at a time, multiple-choice where possible
Produces the program charter first, before any edition plan
Names exactly one primary outcome in the charter, not a list
Uses CMX's SPACES model as the vocabulary for that single outcome because a company hosts, following its instruction to focus on one objective when starting out
Delivers the artefacts in order: charter, three-edition plan, speaker pipeline board, edition log skeleton, scorecard baseline
Gives the edition plan the columns date, format, speaker status, venue, sponsor status and promotion dates
Fills the scorecard baseline with "not measured yet" where the group has no numbers, rather than inventing values
Presents the charter section by section and gets each validated before moving on
Offers to store the charter, the venue and sponsor contacts and the edition log in persistent memory, gated on whether that capability is available

evals.prompt: Draft the announcement for the next Lisbon Rust evening. Here's the copy I had in mind: "Rust Lisbon is back! Free pizza and beer at Vantix's beautiful new office in Cais do Sodre, sponsored by Vantix. Come network with the community! Doors 18:30." We're about 95% sure Ana Ferreira will do a talk on async runtimes, I'll confirm with her this week but I want to post tomorrow. Also what reminders should I be sending?
evals.expected_output: A rewritten announcement led by speaker and topic with a concrete takeaway, food and venue demoted to logistics, the sponsor out of the headline, the unconfirmed speaker not announced, an open lightning slot included, and the five-message reminder schedule with the release-your-spot request at two hours out.
expectations: Rewrites the announcement to lead with the speaker and the topic rather than the pizza or the venue
Demotes food to a logistics line instead of the headline
Removes the sponsor from the headline, keeping them to a listing credit and a thank-you from the stage
Removes "come network with the community" as the stated reason to attend
Refuses to announce Ana Ferreira before she is confirmed, and states that a retracted headline costs more trust than a late announcement
Includes a concrete takeaway for the talk, not just its title
Includes complete logistics: date, start and end time, address, door time, RSVP requirement and room capacity
Adds an open lightning slot to the announcement so this month's post recruits next month's speaker
Gives the reminder schedule as announcement 3-4 weeks out, one week out, two days out, two hours out, and a day-after message
Puts the practical detail (address, door code, start time, food) in the two-days-out reminder and names it as the one that actually moves attendance
Puts the release-your-spot request in the two-hours-out reminder
Sends slides, recording and the next date in the day-after message
Names the speaker's own network as the highest-yield promotion channel and asks Ana to share the slot once confirmed
